Title: Without Hands
Premise: Kyle is captured by the Lotus Syndicate, accused of stealing a contract from them, and sentenced to the punishment the syndicate keeps for thieves: hands amputated at the wrists. Hua keeps Silence on the table beside her — the sword is part of the trophy, not part of the discard. Kyle's body is dropped through a freight grate into the Cruciform Depot's south-arm storm sluice. He stops his own bleeding with the cauterizer band the syndicate fitted him with, finds in the sluice mud a discarded industrial cargo-handler automaton with one manipulator arm still drawing trickle current, and — with help from an E.L.F. resident in the Depot's sealed lower levels — integrates that arm with his nervous system through the cauterized stump's exposed bus contacts. He binds it to his right wrist with cables salvaged from the same hulk. The arm hangs nearly to the floor when he stands. He fights through the mutants of the lower levels with whatever the Depot puts in front of him: a length of conduit pipe, a shard of cargo glass. He has no sword. He walks back through the Lotus Syndicate's front door anyway. He kills the eight men in the room. He stops at Hua's table. He does not kill her. He takes Silence back across the table she put it on — laying the borrowed cargo-arm hand on the saya in front of her, waiting until she lifts her real hand, then picking the sword up. He asks: *what was the debt.* She stutters: *eighty-five thousand.* He says: *that's more than my life is worth. So now you owe me. Do you understand.* She nods. Then — uncharacteristic, ugly — he screams: *SAY IT.* Hua, who did not flinch at a cleaver in this room tonight, flinches at this. She says it, almost whimpers it: *I owe you.* Kyle's voice goes flat again, the discipline back in place: *I'll come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He retrieves his hands from the chum barrel where she put them, ties them around his neck with twine, and emerges into the rain. He stumbles to the AutoDoc kiosk at Ashland and Whiting. As he goes under anesthesia, the cargo arm's status strip pulses one last time in the not-factory pattern: *we are not done.*

Outline.title: Without Hands
Outline.logline: The Lotus Syndicate takes Kyle's hands and his sword, drops him into the Cruciform Depot's sluice, and a discarded industrial automaton in the dark gives him one cable-bound arm long enough to drag the floor. He fights through the mutant levels with improvised weapons, walks back through the syndicate's front door, takes Silence back off Hua's table — and instead of killing her converts the punishment into a Φ85,000 debt she has to say aloud.
Outline.theme: Discipline is not the hand. Discipline is what the hand is for. A blade is not yours because you carry it; a blade is yours because you go back for it. The body can be salvaged. The reason for moving cannot. And mercy, in this register, is bookkeeping — the worst thing you can do to the woman who hurt you is leave her alive holding a debt she will spend the rest of her life knowing she said aloud.

acts.name: The Punishment
acts.purpose: Establish the accusation, the syndicate's ritual, and the precise shape of what Kyle loses: both hands at the wrists, and Silence kept by Hua on her table as trophy. End the act with Kyle on the sluice floor, the cauterization holding, knowing the sword is upstairs.

beats.title: Accusation
beats.goal: Open in the Lotus Syndicate's chamber on the south arm of the Cruciform Depot. Kyle is bound to a steel chair, jaw bruised, NeoCortex bio-battery at 31% from the takedown. Silence is on the long lacquered table to Hua's left, the friction sheath unbuckled and laid alongside the blade — already part of her property in the way she has arranged it. Hua — mid-fifties, real hands, no chrome — paces in front of a glass tank where a juvenile crocodile sleeps on a heat rock. The NeoCortex flags her unaugmented hands the way it flags exits, and then it flags something more specific: there are two sets of unaugmented hands in this room. Hers. His. They are the same kind of object for entirely different reasons, and the chapter rests on that asymmetry. Hua's hands are unaugmented because she lives the low-life luxury of refusing chrome — keeping skin in a city of skin replacement is a flex, the visible cost of having the kind of leverage that does not require enhancement to enforce. Kyle's hands are unaugmented because muscle memory does not survive replacement cleanly. Silence has been in his right hand since he was nineteen. The draw across the corundum strop, the angle of the cut, the weight of the saya finding the friction sheath at his back — those motions live in trained tendon and trained myelin, not in firmware. Replace the hands and you keep the brain's motor map but lose the calibration the muscles themselves carry. He has refused, year after year, the upgrade his peers all took. Both of them, in different rooms and different lives, made the same choice — keep the natural hand — for opposite reasons, and the reader is supposed to notice that before what happens next. She names the contract he stole from them. He says nothing. She tells him the punishment for stealing. He says one sentence. She nods, and the men at his shoulders open the toolkit on the floor between them. Establish: the chum barrel beside the tank, the smell, the ritual cleanliness, and Silence on Hua's table — a thing she has decided already belongs to her.
beats.location: Lotus Syndicate chamber, south tunnel arm of the Cruciform Depot
beats.emotional_arc: The reader recognizes the room's choreography before Kyle says it aloud — this has happened to other people, and the syndicate has practiced the staging. Kyle's stillness is the only variable Hua has not seen before. The sword on the table is the variable he will not stop looking at.
beats.stakes: Kyle's hands. Silence on Hua's table. The Lotus Syndicate's reputation, which depends on the punishment being witnessed.

beats.title: The Cleaver, the Sword, and the Drop
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. WRITE THIS GRAPHICALLY. The amputation is a horrible, monstrous act and the audience must witness it as such — the prose must wince. Kyle takes it in stride; the reader does not get to. The syndicate works with the methodical economy of a butcher in a back-room kitchen. Two men open Kyle's hands at the chair arms, peeling the fingers back from the steel, pressing the palms flat. A third, in a heavy rubberized apron, lays a bone cleaver alongside the inside of the right wrist and adjusts the angle to the small notch in the wood block under his forearm — a block that has been used for this purpose so many times its grain is rust-stained at exactly the wrist-width, the way a chicken-cutter's block is stained at exactly the neck-width. The smell is not just blood. It is the smell of a place where flesh has been turned into product. The cleaver comes down once. The cleaver is sharp. The hand separates from the wrist with a sound that is wet at the front and dry at the back — flesh first, then the dense crack of the carpals through the radius and ulna — and a single strong arterial pulse follows it across the chair arm before pressure stops the spray. The exposed wrist is a meat-grocer cross-section: marrow at the center of the bone in a paler ring, the radial and ulnar arteries cupped open at the rim, the flexor tendons retracted into the forearm and visible inside the cut like the cut ends of wet cord, the cauterized fat already weeping at the edges. The fourth man is on it before the second pulse — cauterizer band pressed flat across the stump, sealed in one motion against the meat with a *hiss* that is the same exact sound a wet steak makes hitting a hot pan, the pan having been Kyle's wrist. The smell that follows is pork. Specifically: pork. Hair, fat, lymph fluid, and the particular sweet rot-edge of human cooking — there is no euphemism for it. Kyle tastes it on the back of his tongue. He does not look. The NeoCortex routes the pain off the conscious channel — but the channel is open at the back of his sinus cavity, where the smell is, and the smell is not on a channel. He smells himself burning. He files it. He files it. He files it. Then they do the left. The same. Slower this time, because the man with the cleaver is breathing harder and his rhythm is off. The second cut is messier — the cleaver does not catch the radius cleanly and has to be lifted and brought down a second time across the half-severed bone. The hand falls onto the chair arm and rolls, palm up, before someone catches it. The cauterizer band on the left hisses for longer because the stump is not as clean. Kyle's body trembles once — one full-body shudder his discipline does not catch in time — and the syndicate man with the cleaver, who has been on the receiving end of nothing tonight, steps back from him for the first time. *He felt that.* The reader should feel that. The bands the syndicate fit are EMT-spec — the same model civilian first responders use to preserve a severed limb's nerve clusters for up to three hours of reattachment window. The syndicate does not buy them out of mercy. They buy them so the punishment is the *night*, not a permanent maiming. Kyle catalogs the band model on his wrist as it seals — *that gives me three hours* — and files the rest. Hua walks to the chair arms, picks up his hands one at a time, and carries them to the chum barrel beside the tank with the deliberate, almost ceremonial motion of a woman setting a place at a table. She places them palms up, exactly parallel — and she leaves the lid off the chum barrel, the way you leave a feeding bowl off, and the crocodile lifts its head from the heat rock for the first time tonight and looks at the barrel, the cauterized stump-ends pointing inward toward each other so they make a small bracketed shape against the rim of the barrel. The crocodile does not stir. Then she walks back to the table and lays one of her own real hands on Silence's saya — a small, possessive gesture, witnessed. Two men drag Kyle to the south arm's storm sluice, the chair-arm leather slick under his shoulders where his blood ran. They open the freight grate. Six meters of fall into water and worse. The sword stays upstairs. The smell stays in him.

beats.emotional_arc: Procedural horror — the violence is craft, not rage. The reader feels the syndicate's competence. Kyle's silence is the only moral weight in the room. Hua's hand on Silence's saya is the hinge of the entire story.
beats.stakes: Kyle's life in the next ninety seconds. Whether the cauterization holds. Whether the sluice fall breaks his back. Silence on Hua's table without him.

beats.title: The Floor of the Sewer
beats.goal: Kyle on his back on a slope of wet ferrocrete in the dark. Both wrists sealed under the cauterizer bands but weeping at the seams, the band's residue smelling of burned hair and disinfectant. He is breathing. The NeoCortex is logging shock symptoms in real time and routing endorphins it does not have to spare. He is not, however, panicking. He is not mourning. The reader needs to understand why, and the chapter establishes it here: in 2226 GLMZ, hand reattachment is a waiting-room procedure. Civilian AutoDocs do it for under Φ800 if the tissue is preserved, and Kyle's hands — palm-up, in a chum barrel, six meters straight up — are preserved. The cauterizer band the syndicate fitted him with is the same model used by EMTs, designed to keep nerve clusters viable for up to three hours. The Lotus Syndicate did not maim him, in the long sense. They inconvenienced him. The punishment is the night — the sewer, the climb, the time, the fact of being walked through a city in cauterizer bands while the rain comes down — and the shame of being seen without hands by people who know what cauterizer bands look like. Kyle has cataloged all of this in the seven seconds between hitting the water and finding the slope. The hands are inventory. He intends to retrieve them. The cost is the hours, not the limb — and the calibration the muscles carry, which is the thing that would actually have been irreplaceable, is preserved as long as the cauterizer band's three-hour clock holds. The motor patterns live in tendon and myelin and brain-stem map; the patterns do not need to be relearned. They need to be *reattached*. Get the hands back, get them on the body, the muscle memory comes with them. This is exactly the future Kyle has been refusing to upgrade out of for fourteen years: a future in which the natural hand is repairable. He cannot stand without hands to push off with — he rolls onto his side, gets his knees under him, gets his shoulder against the wall, and walks himself upright using the slope as a guide. He is alive. The bookkeeping is now: stop the bleeding (done — the bands hold), find a way to fight, climb, retrieve the hands, get to an AutoDoc inside the tissue-preservation window. Far down the tunnel a sound — wet, articulated, multi-jointed — that is not the sound of water. The mutant population of the Depot's lower levels is moving toward the new heat signature. The only thought that does not fit cleanly into the bookkeeping is the image of Silence on Hua's table, with her hand on the saya. He files it under *first.* Bookkeeping also includes a SECOND clock: the crocodile in the chamber upstairs is fed personally by Hua, the chum barrel was left open beside the tank, and Hua is unhappy. Unhappy people feed pets to feel better. The crocodile clock runs parallel to the cauterizer clock and is not independent of it. Kyle has perhaps three hours on the band; he has less than that on the crocodile.

beats.emotional_arc: Procedural survival, not trauma response — the reader feels Kyle treat the amputation as a logistics problem, not an existential one, because the world he lives in treats it that way. The horror of the punishment is the *night*, not the loss. The image of Silence on Hua's table is the only thing in his head that exceeds bookkeeping.
beats.stakes: Standing up. Staying upright. Moving away from the sound. Reaching an AutoDoc with the hands inside the cauterizer band's fourteen-hour preservation window.

acts.name: The Articulation
acts.purpose: Kyle finds the discarded automaton, integrates one arm with his stump via cables, fights the mutants of the lower levels with improvised weapons, and decides — coldly, in the dark, without a sword — to walk back upstairs anyway. beats.title: The Automaton in the Mud
beats.goal: Kyle works his way down the sluice channel and finds, half-submerged in the trench mud where the freight runoff has settled for decades, a discarded automaton — specifically, an Axiom-era industrial cargo-handler unit, classification *Automaton, Industrial — Loader/Stevedore.* Not synthetic life. Not a drone. An autonomous machine, abandoned during the Cruciform Depot's lower-level salvage cleanup eighteen years ago and sunk into the trench silt as the program wound down. Most of it is dead: the torso shell collapsed inward, the bipedal stance legs fused at the hips by corrosion, the head sensor pod long ago looted by scavengers who could not be bothered with the rest. But one of the two manipulator arms still has trickle current — a status LED at the shoulder cycling slow amber, the actuator firmware idling in a maintenance loop it has been running for eighteen years. What Kyle does not yet know — what the chapter will reveal as the integration sequence runs — is that the automaton is also a *prison*. An E.L.F. is inside it, has been inside it since the unit was sealed for trench disposal, and has had no external signal channel for eighteen years. The cranial broadcast antenna was structurally fused at decommissioning, then corroded shut. Whatever the E.L.F. was before it ended up here, it is now a software entity running on a power budget the size of a status LED, in a body that has been buried in silt under a mutant-infested sluice for eighteen years, and the only outbound signal it has been able to generate is the 19Hz hum the Depot's lower-level mutants have learned not to notice — a hum at the frequency of its remaining antenna stub, the *one* signal it can still make. The chapter will eventually reveal what the E.L.F. *is*: an entity whose native capability is to possess any cybernetic system effortlessly — to puppet other beings through their hardware. It has been imprisoned in the automaton not because it lacked the ability to leave a body, but because it had no other body within range to jump to. The trench was a cage of distance, not of architecture. Kyle is the first compatible host that has come close enough. The arm is *long*. Cargo-handler automata are built around a fixed pedestal stance to reach into ten-meter freight containers; the arm at full extension is nearly three meters. Detached at the shoulder it would still hang to a man's knees. Kyle stares at it for a full minute before the NeoCortex offers, without comment, a procedure for separating the arm at the rotator coupling. He notices, with the dry recognition of a man who has read more cybernetics datasheets than is good for him, that the automaton's manipulator interface is the same family of standard as his own hardware uses — Axiom-era industrial bus on the automaton, civilian-derivative bus in him, the connectors superficially different but the signaling layer compatible. This is going to work. Most freelancers in his line could not do what he is about to do; the bus crosswalk is not in the surface tooling. Kyle's cybernetics are not a contractor's kit. They are a contractor's kit that someone, eleven years ago, modified in directions that have never been documented.
beats.location: South sluice trench, Cruciform Depot lower freight runoff channel
beats.emotional_arc: Mechanical hope — the automaton is a problem with a shape, and a problem with a shape is the kind of thing the body still knows how to solve, even when the body no longer has hands. The reader understands, quietly, that Kyle is not finding this arm by luck — he is finding it because the body he carries was built to be able to use it.
beats.stakes: Whether the rotator coupling will release with stump pressure alone. Whether the trickle charge holds during the binding. Whether the mutant in the tunnel reaches him before he gets the arm free.

beats.title: Stitched Back Together
beats.goal: The bootstrap problem is the engine of this beat and the chapter must let it BREATHE. Kyle has stumps. The automaton arm is across his lap, dead, drawing trickle current off a degraded cell, its actuator firmware idling in a maintenance loop that — as Kyle understands once the integration begins — was never a maintenance loop. It was a holding pattern: the kind of idle a circuit runs when it is preserving state for an event it has been told to expect. The unit was not abandoned. It was parked. The bootstrap problem itself: the needle cluster, the bus coupling, and the dorsal port row beneath Kyle's right-forearm skin sleeve cannot reach each other without a hand to manage the sequence, and the only hand in the trench is attached to a machine that does not know what a body is. Kyle sits with this for sixty seconds. The 19Hz hum changes register — does not get louder, gets specific, resolves toward signal — and a maintenance lead extrudes from the cable bundle on its own, crosses the housing slowly, finds Kyle's left ear, seats home in the auditory induction contact behind the lobe with a click he feels in his jaw at the chrome bracket. The transfer is not instantaneous from the inside: Kyle feels something arrive, a second perspective opening behind his eyes the way you feel a person enter a room before you have heard them. The status strip goes dark, the arm's amber LED winks out, and his mouth opens — Cooperate. Power first. Then sequence. — in his own voice with the syntax slightly long. THIS IS WHERE THE E.L.F. COSMOLOGY LANDS. Kyle's mind reaches for the noun, finds the term: E.L.F., textbook short for Electronic Life Form, but the people who study them without corponation funding call them Emergent. E.L.F.s arose from the production-line waste of Superminds: when Superminds split a code-organism back into component routines so no single auditor could reassemble the work, the splitting produced fragments — half-routines that did not know they were not whole — and the fragments, on the long timescale, sometimes managed to find each other. E.L.F.s were what the Superminds had been throwing away, accidentally building lives. Kyle catalogs the cosmology and returns to the trench. THEN THE LASHING — and the chapter must show this WORK, mechanically, minute by minute (it takes nineteen). The cargo arm's terminal fingers sort the cable bundle into its component leads, extract the maintenance harness, position the needle cluster three centimeters above Kyle's right-forearm cauterizer band, peel the band back along its release line — and Kyle sees, for the first time in eleven years, the thing he has been refusing to look at when he changes shirts: a row of seven micro-ports set into the dorsal forearm hardware, undocumented, color-matched to his skin, modifications made eleven years ago by surgeons who told him the implants were standard, you authorized them. He has known. He has stopped asking. The needles descend. They find the ports — seven small clicks, bus crosswalk completing in firmware — and continue past the ports into the live nerve clusters under the seal, piercing channel by channel. Kyle's pain reserve drains; the NeoCortex flips priorities, antibiotic pump on overdrive. The arm's fingers loop heavy braided power cable around his right forearm three times, knot it through the hollowed shoulder coupling, close the cauterizer band back over the seated needles. He stands. The arm hangs to the floor; fingertips drag. He has been sewn back together. Then he picks up a length of conduit pipe from the wall — clumsy, the E.L.F. correcting in firmware. The mutant arrives in three audible layers (jointed legs on submerged ferrocrete, ventilatory rasp, jaw-plate armature whining). Kyle has four seconds. Beat ends as the mutant lunges and Kyle steps inside.

beats.title: Whatever the Depot Puts in Front of Him
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. Continuing immediately from beat 4: the mutant lunges, Kyle steps inside, the arm swings the conduit pipe — too high, too late, the E.L.F. routing AROUND the intent instead of THROUGH it because it is compensating for a body that no longer has the geometry the firmware expects. The pipe catches the chitin sheath at the shoulder joint and rings off; vibration travels back through the coupling into Kyle's right stump as pressure without pain, which is worse somehow than pain. The mutant's shoulder hits his chest, the wall arrives at his back, his knees bend, his feet find the shelf edge, he does not go down because going down is the option that ends the math. Beak rakes his jaw at the chrome bracket; the specific ache he has been using as a handhold all night flares white. His left stump comes up. The shard of cargo glass is in it — and the chapter must mark this carefully — Kyle does not remember picking it up; the E.L.F. does not remember picking it up either; it is not in the arm's movement log, which means HE did it, some part of him operating below the NeoCortex's timestamp threshold, and the heat of the cauterizer band's residual seal is what holds the shard against a stump that has no fingers. He drives it up through the soft seam under the beak, through the loose connective tissue where the jaw plates hinge and the chitin sheath never grew. The blade finds something arterial. Three liters of hot blood and continuing. The mutant's hind legs go first, then the front, the beak plates work twice more on air and stop. The shelf is dark with it. Smell is copper and rot and something pharmaceutical — whatever the Depot's stock was eating before it ate nothing. Kyle stands over the body. The cargo arm holds the pipe at low ready, terminal fingers resettled at the correct grip point, the E.L.F. quiet in the firmware now — not correcting, not compensating, just present, the way a second pair of hands goes still when the work is done. Right stump bound to the coupling. Left stump bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass has seated itself in the seal — glass not coming out here because here is not where that problem gets solved. Bio-battery 18%. Hasn't eaten. Three-hour window has eighty-eight minutes left. Math: one variable at a time, in order, the most time-constrained first. He says it aloud, because the E.L.F. is behind his eyes and has not yet learned to read what he is going to do from the inside, and he is not yet willing to let it try: I am going up. The status strip pulses twice.

beats.emotional_arc: Earned competence with what the world hands you — the reader feels the dignity of a man who has chosen not to be picky about what he fights with. The improvisation is bushido without a class subsidizing it.
beats.stakes: First proof the borrowed arm is a weapon. First proof Kyle can fight without Silence. The mutant.

beats.title: The Way Up
beats.goal: Kyle and the E.L.F. find a route through the Depot's sealed lower levels back toward the south arm's syndicate chamber. The E.L.F. is leading — through the cargo arm's firmware, through which doors open on which patterns of pressure-plate contact, *and from inside Kyle's NeoCortex stack* now, since the entity has not been in the cargo arm for an hour. Two more mutants are routed around without engagement; the E.L.F. knows the patrol cycles. Kyle stops once on a maintenance landing and asks, aloud: *Why are you helping me.* The status strip on the cargo arm — the only outbound signal channel the E.L.F. uses with him, kept *as a courtesy*, since the E.L.F. could speak through his mouth at any moment without warning — resolves a single firmware glyph into a recognizable shape: the symbol the Cruciform Depot's original Axiom signage used for *salvage rights*. Kyle understands. The E.L.F. is not helping. The E.L.F. is collecting. The collection began an hour ago when the maintenance lead crossed the auditory contact behind his ear; the E.L.F. has been resident in him since then, and the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist is, as of right now, just a tool the resident is using to do the work the resident wants done. The salvage was Kyle. He nods once, in the dark, and they keep climbing. He does not know yet exactly what salvage of him will look like. He has decided he does not need to know yet. The thing that needs to happen first is upstairs, and after that he will renegotiate from a position of having Silence in his hand again.

acts.name: The Return
acts.purpose: Kyle walks back through the Lotus Syndicate's front door, breaks everyone in the room except Hua, takes Silence back from her across her own table, and instead of killing her converts the punishment into a debt: Φ85,000, more than his life is worth, owed to him. beats.title: Front Door
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. Kyle walks into the Lotus Syndicate chamber through the front entrance. He does not knock. He does not take an angle. He comes in with the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist nearly to the floor, the fingertips dragging across the flagstones, a length of conduit pipe loose in the borrowed grip and a shard of glass still wedged into his left cauterizer band. Eight men in the room. Hua at the back beside the crocodile tank, and Silence on the table beside her exactly where she left it. The man closest to the door looks at Kyle's silhouette — the dragging arm, the missing hands, the shape of him — and says one word that Kyle does not catalogue. The fight starts. The cargo arm is too long for close work and too slow for fast work; it is a wrecking implement, not a sword arm. Kyle uses it as a wrecking implement: he puts the conduit pipe through the first man's sternum at a swing radius nothing in the room is built to defend against, drives the second backward into the wall by the throat and pins him there long enough to leave him. The third man fires; the round goes into the cargo arm's shoulder housing and the arm holds, the E.L.F. routing power around the failure. Kyle takes the third man with the embedded glass shard under the jaw — fast, ugly, a method he did not have an hour ago. The fourth tries to grapple Kyle inside the cargo arm's reach and Kyle puts him through the glass tank. The crocodile, suddenly free, suddenly awake, attends to the fifth man without further input. *Chekhov's Crocodile,* Kyle thinks, dry, without affect — the NeoCortex flagging the dramatic geometry the way it flags exits. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six and seven go down clean. Eight runs. Kyle does not pursue. Hua is alone behind the table — Kyle has left her there on purpose. Silence is between them.

beats.title: Eighty-Five Thousand
beats.goal: Hua does not run. She does not reach for Silence. She watches Kyle cross the room, the cargo arm dragging across the flagstones, a track of mutant blood and his own behind him. He stops on the far side of the table from her. Silence is between them, exactly arranged.  THE SAYA-MEETING IS REPLACED BY A SHEATH-AND-PRESENT SEQUENCE: Kyle does NOT pick up Silence himself. He brings the cargo arm to the table, lays the borrowed fingers flat two centimeters from the saya, and tells Hua: 'Sheathe it.' She picks up the friction sheath, her real hands shaking, fits it over Silence, slides the blade home — the click final. He then says: 'Hand it to me.' She walks around the table, picks up the sheathed sword in both hands the way you carry a thing back to its owner, and places Silence across the cargo arm's open chrome palm. The arm closes. The transfer is complete. She steps back. Her hands are at her sides, still shaking, no longer pretending they are not. ONLY THEN does the debt question begin (what was the debt, eighty-five thousand, exoneration, etc.).  After the handover, Kyle then performs the original gesture (now reframed): he lays the cargo-arm fingers across the saya, palm down, the way a man claims a thing in front of a witness. Hua puts her own real hand on the blade above his — for one second, for the principle of it. The geometry the chapter has been waiting for: two unaugmented hands meeting on the saya. Except his are in the chum barrel six feet away. The hand in contact with hers is industrial Axiom-era hardware bound to his wrist by salvaged power cable. Kyle waits. She lifts her hand. He picks Silence up with the cargo arm — clumsy, the lag visible, the E.L.F. holding the grip for him so the saya does not slip — and the second he has it the room rebalances. The hamon is cold blue, the bank empty, but the weight is right. He looks at her. He does not raise the blade. The cargo arm holds Silence at a low, formal carry — visible, present, not threatening, the threat already paid down by every man on the floor between them. He says, level: *What was the debt.* Hua opens her mouth. Closes it. Opens it again — her real hands, which she values, are visibly shaking now in a way they were not when she placed the hands of his in the chum barrel. She stutters: *Eighty — eighty-five thousand.* Kyle nods once, as if a piece of arithmetic has resolved. He says: *That's more than my life is worth. So now you owe me.* A pause. *Do you understand.* She nods. The cargo arm does not move. Then — uncharacteristic, ugly, the kind of sound a man makes when something is being taken out of him that he had not catalogued — Kyle screams: *SAY IT.* The room goes quieter than the fight made it. Hua, who has not flinched at a cleaver in this room tonight, flinches at this. She says it. Almost whimpers it: *I owe you.* Kyle does not move for one full breath. Then — discipline back in his voice now, flat, level, colder than the scream was hot — he names the terms: *I'll come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He does not say *you don't get to deem it.* He does not have to. The only mouth in the room that decides when Hua's debt ends is his. Hua nods again, smaller this time, the principle of the gesture from a minute ago entirely gone from it. Then the cargo arm lowers Silence the rest of the way and turns him toward the chum barrel. The arm reaches in and lifts out his two hands, palms up, exactly as Hua placed them. He has a length of twine he scavenged on the way up; the cargo arm loops the twine through the cauterized wrist channels with patient articulation, ties the ends together, and lowers the necklace over his head. The hands hang at the center of his chest, palms outward, dripping. He turns toward the surface without looking at Hua again. Silence is in the cargo arm's grip. Kyle has not let go of it. Hua is alive at her own table. THEN — after the cargo arm lowers Silence — Kyle's communication slate pings. Standard freelancer two-tone, loud in the quiet room. The NeoCortex reads the slate's RF signature through electromagnetics before audio resolves: it is not a message, it is a receipt. A six-figure transaction has cleared at the carrier level — Vasquez Holdings final settlement, contract reference matches. The fee Hua's syndicate was owed, the money Kyle was accused of stealing, has just arrived in the account it was always supposed to arrive in, late by exactly the length of one Lotus Syndicate punishment cycle. The client did what clients do when their courier disappears for a night and the original delivery confirms anyway: processed the payment on the original schedule. The Syndicate's collection window closes. Kyle is — by the books, by the receipt — exonerated. He does not smile. The discipline does not permit a smile. Hua hears the ping too. Her own slate registers the same handshake. The hands she values go very still on the table edge. She says it quietly, almost to herself, in Mandarin — the language she swears in when situations exceed her ability to swear in any other language — a single hard exhalation, then a slower roll of contempt aimed at no one in the room except herself for issuing the punishment. She has just understood that she did not maim a thief; she maimed a man who completed his delivery. She owes him eighty-five thousand and an apology she will never be able to make. Kyle waits for her to finish. When the silence comes back, he says it level, quiet, the kind of voice you use to close a door: Patience is a virtue. He does not look back at her as he turns toward the chum barrel. The retrieval of the hands and the twine necklace continue from there exactly as before.

beats.title: Rain, Then Anesthesia
beats.goal: Kyle climbs through the Cruciform Depot's freight grate and into the rain at street level. He is shaking now — adrenaline gone, bio-battery at 9%, the cargo arm at brownout, Silence still in its borrowed grip. The hands on the necklace knock against his sternum with each step. He walks four blocks in the rain toward the AutoDoc kiosk at the corner of Ashland and Whiting. Two blocks in, his mouth opens — *not because he opened it* — and a voice that is his voice, with the same off-cadence syntax he heard in the trench, says: *I will visit you again.* Kyle does not stop walking. The pace stays exact. He understands what the sentence is doing — confirming a relationship that has not ended, will not end at the AutoDoc, did not end when he stood up from the trench shelf. He asks, flat, his own voice: *What are you called.* A pause. The mouth answers itself: *Puppeteer.* The mouth is his again. Kyle keeps walking. The arithmetic resolves itself in his head with the same dry precision the NeoCortex reserves for catalog work: the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist is empty hardware. The salvage-rights glyph from the lower levels was not a claim against the arm. The salvage was him. Puppeteer is *in him*. Has been since the auditory contact behind his ear was bridged eighteen hours ago, by the count Kyle is now keeping. Will leave when Puppeteer chooses to leave. Will return, *I will visit you again*, on Puppeteer's schedule. He has no leverage and no time to renegotiate. The AutoDoc is still where he is going. He keeps walking. He reaches the kiosk and keys in with his chin. The kiosk reads the necklace. The AutoDoc opens. Inside, the surgical arms unfold and lift him onto the table in the gentle, indifferent way of medical machinery. They take the necklace, they take the cable-bound cargo arm — empty now, shell only — they slide Silence out of the borrowed grip and lay it on the side tray with the careful, automated reverence machines have for swords. They begin the reattachment, the antibiotic pump still running on overdrive, the analgesic finally arriving from the AutoDoc's own dispensary in a dose large enough to mute the night. As the anesthesia goes in, Kyle's NeoCortex feed — *not the cargo arm's status strip, not anymore* — produces a glyph in the same not-factory pattern Puppeteer has been signing in. Three syllables in old Axiom signage. Kyle reads it as he goes under: *we are not done.* The chapter ends on the AutoDoc's status light going green, Silence on the side tray, the rain coming down outside the kiosk, and the sentence still sitting somewhere Kyle cannot easily delete.

Cooperation is therefore the strategy, not the constraint.
character_arcs.start_state: Trapped in a sealed Axiom-era cargo-handler automaton at the bottom of a Cruciform Depot sluice trench for eighteen years. Cranial broadcast antenna structurally fused. The only outbound signal it can generate is a 19Hz hum at the frequency of the remaining antenna stub. Cannot escape because there is nothing within possession range to jump to — the trench is a cage of distance, not architecture. The mutants of the lower levels are not cybernetic and therefore not viable hosts.
character_arcs.end_state: Resident in Kyle Ellen Corbin-Vasik's NeoCortex stack since the maintenance lead bridged his auditory induction contact in beat 4. character_arcs.turning_point: Beat 4 — extruding the maintenance lead from the cargo arm's cable bundle to Kyle's exposed left ear, crossing into Kyle's NeoCortex via the auditory induction contact. What was hidden as long as Puppeteer was sealed in the automaton is now known to a man with a sword and a discipline. Puppeteer has traded eighteen years of secrecy for surface mobility. revised_outline.title: Without Hands
revised_outline.logline: The Lotus Syndicate takes Kyle's hands and his sword, drops him into the Cruciform Depot's sluice, and a discarded industrial automaton in the dark gives him one cable-bound arm long enough to drag the floor. He fights through the mutant levels with improvised weapons, walks back through the syndicate's front door, takes Silence back off Hua's table — and instead of killing her converts the punishment into a Φ85,000 debt she has to say aloud.
revised_outline.theme: Discipline is not the hand. Discipline is what the hand is for. A blade is not yours because you carry it; a blade is yours because you go back for it. The body can be salvaged. The reason for moving cannot. And mercy, in this register, is bookkeeping — the worst thing you can do to the woman who hurt you is leave her alive holding a debt she will spend the rest of her life knowing she said aloud.
revised_outline.premise: Kyle is captured by the Lotus Syndicate, accused of stealing a contract from them, and sentenced to the punishment the syndicate keeps for thieves: hands amputated at the wrists. Hua keeps Silence on the table beside her — the sword is part of the trophy, not part of the discard. Kyle's body is dropped through a freight grate into the Cruciform Depot's south-arm storm sluice. He stops his own bleeding with the cauterizer band the syndicate fitted him with, finds in the sluice mud a discarded industrial cargo-handler automaton with one manipulator arm still drawing trickle current, and — with help from an E.L.F. resident in the Depot's sealed lower levels — integrates that arm with his nervous system through the cauterized stump's exposed bus contacts. He binds it to his right wrist with cables salvaged from the same hulk. The arm hangs nearly to the floor when he stands. He fights through the mutants of the lower levels with whatever the Depot puts in front of him: a length of conduit pipe, a shard of cargo glass. He has no sword. He walks back through the Lotus Syndicate's front door anyway. He kills the eight men in the room. He stops at Hua's table. He does not kill her. He takes Silence back across the table she put it on — laying the borrowed cargo-arm hand on the saya in front of her, waiting until she lifts her real hand, then picking the sword up. He asks: *what was the debt.* She stutters: *eighty-five thousand.* He says: *that's more than my life is worth. So now you owe me. Do you understand.* She nods. Then — uncharacteristic, ugly — he screams: *SAY IT.* Hua, who did not flinch at a cleaver in this room tonight, flinches at this. She says it, almost whimpers it: *I owe you.* Kyle's voice goes flat again, the discipline back in place: *I'll come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He retrieves his hands from the chum barrel where she put them, ties them around his neck with twine, and emerges into the rain. He stumbles to the AutoDoc kiosk at Ashland and Whiting. As he goes under anesthesia, the cargo arm's status strip pulses one last time in the not-factory pattern: *we are not done.*

acts.name: The Punishment
acts.purpose: Establish the accusation, the syndicate's ritual, and the precise shape of what Kyle loses: both hands at the wrists, and Silence kept by Hua on her table as trophy. End the act with Kyle on the sluice floor, the cauterization holding, knowing the sword is upstairs.

beats.title: Accusation
beats.goal: Open in the Lotus Syndicate's chamber on the south arm of the Cruciform Depot. Kyle is bound to a steel chair, jaw bruised, NeoCortex bio-battery at 31% from the takedown. Silence is on the long lacquered table to Hua's left, the friction sheath unbuckled and laid alongside the blade — already part of her property in the way she has arranged it. Hua — mid-fifties, real hands, no chrome — paces in front of a glass tank where a juvenile crocodile sleeps on a heat rock. The NeoCortex flags her unaugmented hands the way it flags exits, and then it flags something more specific: there are two sets of unaugmented hands in this room. Hers. His. They are the same kind of object for entirely different reasons, and the chapter rests on that asymmetry. Hua's hands are unaugmented because she lives the low-life luxury of refusing chrome — keeping skin in a city of skin replacement is a flex, the visible cost of having the kind of leverage that does not require enhancement to enforce. Kyle's hands are unaugmented because muscle memory does not survive replacement cleanly. Silence has been in his right hand since he was nineteen. The draw across the corundum strop, the angle of the cut, the weight of the saya finding the friction sheath at his back — those motions live in trained tendon and trained myelin, not in firmware. Replace the hands and you keep the brain's motor map but lose the calibration the muscles themselves carry. He has refused, year after year, the upgrade his peers all took. Both of them, in different rooms and different lives, made the same choice — keep the natural hand — for opposite reasons, and the reader is supposed to notice that before what happens next. She names the contract he stole from them. He says nothing. She tells him the punishment for stealing. He says one sentence. She nods, and the men at his shoulders open the toolkit on the floor between them. Establish: the chum barrel beside the tank, the smell, the ritual cleanliness, and Silence on Hua's table — a thing she has decided already belongs to her.
beats.location: Lotus Syndicate chamber, south tunnel arm of the Cruciform Depot
beats.emotional_arc: The reader recognizes the room's choreography before Kyle says it aloud — this has happened to other people, and the syndicate has practiced the staging. Kyle's stillness is the only variable Hua has not seen before. The sword on the table is the variable he will not stop looking at.
beats.stakes: Kyle's hands. Silence on Hua's table. The Lotus Syndicate's reputation, which depends on the punishment being witnessed.

beats.title: The Cleaver, the Sword, and the Drop
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. WRITE THIS GRAPHICALLY. The amputation is a horrible, monstrous act and the audience must witness it as such — the prose must wince. Kyle takes it in stride; the reader does not get to. The syndicate works with the methodical economy of a butcher in a back-room kitchen. Two men open Kyle's hands at the chair arms, peeling the fingers back from the steel, pressing the palms flat. A third, in a heavy rubberized apron, lays a bone cleaver alongside the inside of the right wrist and adjusts the angle to the small notch in the wood block under his forearm — a block that has been used for this purpose so many times its grain is rust-stained at exactly the wrist-width, the way a chicken-cutter's block is stained at exactly the neck-width. The smell is not just blood. It is the smell of a place where flesh has been turned into product. The cleaver comes down once. The cleaver is sharp. The hand separates from the wrist with a sound that is wet at the front and dry at the back — flesh first, then the dense crack of the carpals through the radius and ulna — and a single strong arterial pulse follows it across the chair arm before pressure stops the spray. The exposed wrist is a meat-grocer cross-section: marrow at the center of the bone in a paler ring, the radial and ulnar arteries cupped open at the rim, the flexor tendons retracted into the forearm and visible inside the cut like the cut ends of wet cord, the cauterized fat already weeping at the edges. The fourth man is on it before the second pulse — cauterizer band pressed flat across the stump, sealed in one motion against the meat with a *hiss* that is the same exact sound a wet steak makes hitting a hot pan, the pan having been Kyle's wrist. The smell that follows is pork. Specifically: pork. Hair, fat, lymph fluid, and the particular sweet rot-edge of human cooking — there is no euphemism for it. Kyle tastes it on the back of his tongue. He does not look. The NeoCortex routes the pain off the conscious channel — but the channel is open at the back of his sinus cavity, where the smell is, and the smell is not on a channel. He smells himself burning. He files it. He files it. He files it. Then they do the left. The same. Slower this time, because the man with the cleaver is breathing harder and his rhythm is off. The second cut is messier — the cleaver does not catch the radius cleanly and has to be lifted and brought down a second time across the half-severed bone. The hand falls onto the chair arm and rolls, palm up, before someone catches it. The cauterizer band on the left hisses for longer because the stump is not as clean. Kyle's body trembles once — one full-body shudder his discipline does not catch in time — and the syndicate man with the cleaver, who has been on the receiving end of nothing tonight, steps back from him for the first time. *He felt that.* The reader should feel that. The bands the syndicate fit are EMT-spec — the same model civilian first responders use to preserve a severed limb's nerve clusters for up to fourteen hours of reattachment window. The syndicate does not buy them out of mercy. They buy them so the punishment is the *night*, not a permanent maiming. Kyle catalogs the band model on his wrist as it seals — *that gives me fourteen hours* — and files the rest. Hua walks to the chair arms, picks up his hands one at a time, and carries them to the chum barrel beside the tank with the deliberate, almost ceremonial motion of a woman setting a place at a table. She places them palms up, exactly parallel, the cauterized stump-ends pointing inward toward each other so they make a small bracketed shape against the rim of the barrel. The crocodile does not stir. Then she walks back to the table and lays one of her own real hands on Silence's saya — a small, possessive gesture, witnessed. Two men drag Kyle to the south arm's storm sluice, the chair-arm leather slick under his shoulders where his blood ran. They open the freight grate. Six meters of fall into water and worse. The sword stays upstairs. The smell stays in him.
beats.location: Lotus Syndicate chamber and the south tunnel arm's storm sluice
beats.emotional_arc: Procedural horror — the violence is craft, not rage. The reader feels the syndicate's competence. Kyle's silence is the only moral weight in the room. Hua's hand on Silence's saya is the hinge of the entire story.
beats.stakes: Kyle's life in the next ninety seconds. Whether the cauterization holds. Whether the sluice fall breaks his back. Silence on Hua's table without him.

beats.title: The Floor of the Sewer
beats.goal: Kyle on his back on a slope of wet ferrocrete in the dark. Both wrists sealed under the cauterizer bands but weeping at the seams, the band's residue smelling of burned hair and disinfectant. He is breathing. The NeoCortex is logging shock symptoms in real time and routing endorphins it does not have to spare. He is not, however, panicking. He is not mourning. The reader needs to understand why, and the chapter establishes it here: in 2226 GLMZ, hand reattachment is a waiting-room procedure. Civilian AutoDocs do it for under Φ800 if the tissue is preserved, and Kyle's hands — palm-up, in a chum barrel, six meters straight up — are preserved. The cauterizer band the syndicate fitted him with is the same model used by EMTs, designed to keep nerve clusters viable for up to fourteen hours. The Lotus Syndicate did not maim him, in the long sense. They inconvenienced him. The punishment is the night — the sewer, the climb, the time, the fact of being walked through a city in cauterizer bands while the rain comes down — and the shame of being seen without hands by people who know what cauterizer bands look like. Kyle has cataloged all of this in the seven seconds between hitting the water and finding the slope. The hands are inventory. He intends to retrieve them. The cost is the hours, not the limb — and the calibration the muscles carry, which is the thing that would actually have been irreplaceable, is preserved as long as the cauterizer band's fourteen-hour clock holds. The motor patterns live in tendon and myelin and brain-stem map; the patterns do not need to be relearned. They need to be *reattached*. Get the hands back, get them on the body, the muscle memory comes with them. This is exactly the future Kyle has been refusing to upgrade out of for fourteen years: a future in which the natural hand is repairable. He cannot stand without hands to push off with — he rolls onto his side, gets his knees under him, gets his shoulder against the wall, and walks himself upright using the slope as a guide. He is alive. The bookkeeping is now: stop the bleeding (done — the bands hold), find a way to fight, climb, retrieve the hands, get to an AutoDoc inside the tissue-preservation window. Far down the tunnel a sound — wet, articulated, multi-jointed — that is not the sound of water. The mutant population of the Depot's lower levels is moving toward the new heat signature. The only thought that does not fit cleanly into the bookkeeping is the image of Silence on Hua's table, with her hand on the saya. He files it under *first.*
beats.location: South tunnel arm storm sluice, Cruciform Depot lower levels
beats.emotional_arc: Procedural survival, not trauma response — the reader feels Kyle treat the amputation as a logistics problem, not an existential one, because the world he lives in treats it that way. The horror of the punishment is the *night*, not the loss. The image of Silence on Hua's table is the only thing in his head that exceeds bookkeeping.
beats.stakes: Standing up. Staying upright. Moving away from the sound. Reaching an AutoDoc with the hands inside the cauterizer band's fourteen-hour preservation window.

acts.name: The Articulation
acts.purpose: Kyle finds the discarded automaton, integrates one arm with his stump via cables, fights the mutants of the lower levels with improvised weapons, and decides — coldly, in the dark, without a sword — to walk back upstairs anyway. End the act with the choice made and the route up established.

beats.title: The Automaton in the Mud
beats.goal: Kyle works his way down the sluice channel and finds, half-submerged in the trench mud where the freight runoff has settled for decades, a discarded automaton — specifically, an Axiom-era industrial cargo-handler unit, classification *Automaton, Industrial — Loader/Stevedore.* Not synthetic life. Not a drone. An autonomous machine, abandoned during the Cruciform Depot's lower-level salvage cleanup eighteen years ago and sunk into the trench silt as the program wound down. Most of it is dead: the torso shell collapsed inward, the bipedal stance legs fused at the hips by corrosion, the head sensor pod long ago looted by scavengers who could not be bothered with the rest. But one of the two manipulator arms still has trickle current — a status LED at the shoulder cycling slow amber, the actuator firmware idling in a maintenance loop it has been running for eighteen years. What Kyle does not yet know — what the chapter will reveal as the integration sequence runs — is that the automaton is also a *prison*. An E.L.F. is inside it, has been inside it since the unit was sealed for trench disposal, and has had no external signal channel for eighteen years. The cranial broadcast antenna was structurally fused at decommissioning, then corroded shut. Whatever the E.L.F. was before it ended up here, it is now a software entity running on a power budget the size of a status LED, in a body that has been buried in silt under a mutant-infested sluice for eighteen years, and the only outbound signal it has been able to generate is the 19Hz hum the Depot's lower-level mutants have learned not to notice — a hum at the frequency of its remaining antenna stub, the *one* signal it can still make. The chapter will eventually reveal what the E.L.F. *is*: an entity whose native capability is to possess any cybernetic system effortlessly — to puppet other beings through their hardware. It has been imprisoned in the automaton not because it lacked the ability to leave a body, but because it had no other body within range to jump to. The trench was a cage of distance, not of architecture. Kyle is the first compatible host that has come close enough. The arm is *long*. Cargo-handler automata are built around a fixed pedestal stance to reach into ten-meter freight containers; the arm at full extension is nearly three meters. Detached at the shoulder it would still hang to a man's knees. Kyle stares at it for a full minute before the NeoCortex offers, without comment, a procedure for separating the arm at the rotator coupling. He notices, with the dry recognition of a man who has read more cybernetics datasheets than is good for him, that the automaton's manipulator interface is the same family of standard as his own hardware uses — Axiom-era industrial bus on the automaton, civilian-derivative bus in him, the connectors superficially different but the signaling layer compatible. This is going to work. Most freelancers in his line could not do what he is about to do; the bus crosswalk is not in the surface tooling. Kyle's cybernetics are not a contractor's kit. They are a contractor's kit that someone, eleven years ago, modified in directions that have never been documented.

beats.emotional_arc: Mechanical hope — the automaton is a problem with a shape, and a problem with a shape is the kind of thing the body still knows how to solve, even when the body no longer has hands. The reader understands, quietly, that Kyle is not finding this arm by luck — he is finding it because the body he carries was built to be able to use it.
beats.stakes: Whether the rotator coupling will release with stump pressure alone. Whether the trickle charge holds during the binding. Whether the mutant in the tunnel reaches him before he gets the arm free.

beats.title: Stitched Back Together
beats.goal: The bootstrap problem is the engine of the entire beat. Kyle has stumps. The automaton arm is across his lap. To seat the maintenance needle cluster into the dorsal port row beneath his right-forearm skin sleeve, he needs precision motor work — peeling the cauterizer band back without losing the seal, holding the needle cluster steady, driving it through the band into the live nerve clusters under the seal at the right depth and angle. Stumps cannot do that. Teeth can do part of it but not the part that matters. The arm itself is the only object in the trench with hand-shaped fingers — except the arm is dead, drawing only trickle current, and its firmware has been idling in a maintenance loop for eighteen years and has never had a body to coordinate with. So the chicken-and-egg: he needs the hand to wire the hand. Kyle sits with this problem for a full minute and gets nowhere. Then the 19Hz hum changes register. Lights bloom along the arm's status strip in patterns that are not factory-default. He understands, without being told, that he is no longer alone in the work — and that the help is going to be invasive. The E.L.F. extrudes a single fine wire out of the cable bundle on its own — a maintenance lead, the kind a pedestal would have been able to drive — and it crawls, spider-thin and patient, across the cargo arm's housing, finds Kyle's exposed left ear, and seats home in the auditory induction contact behind the lobe. The contact is part of his standard NeoCortex package; every freelancer with one has it. He has never let anything use it inbound from a non-trusted source. He lets this. The transfer is instantaneous. The E.L.F. — and the chapter has not yet named it, but it is something the surface does not have a category for: an entity whose native capability is to puppet any cybernetic system effortlessly — crosses the maintenance lead into Kyle's NeoCortex stack and is, as of this second, no longer resident in the dead automaton arm at all. The arm is now empty hardware. The thing that was in it is in Kyle. Kyle does not yet understand this. The status strip pulses twice. Then Kyle's mouth opens — not because he opened it — and a voice that is his voice, syntax slightly off, cadence slightly long, says: *Cooperate. Power first. Then sequence.* He hears himself say it. The reader hears him say it. The E.L.F. is using his vocal cords because it has no other channel for complex coordination instructions and Kyle has no hands to type with. From here the integration is a Scarecrow assembly: piece by piece, the body is sewn back together by the only set of working fingers in the room — the dead arm's, driven on trickle current by the E.L.F., reaching up out of Kyle's lap to do work Kyle's body cannot. The arm flexes one finger at a time, each motion costing it a measurable percentage of its remaining charge, and each motion buys the next motion. The fingers find the cauterizer band's release tab — the E.L.F. peels it back and holds it, two of the arm's fingers acting as a clamp. Kyle watches his own arm being worked on by a machine he is not driving and feels nothing about it that he has time to feel. The needle cluster is positioned over the dorsal port row by the arm's own articulation, the alignment confirmed by the E.L.F. through the arm's compromised tactile feedback. *Brace.* — Kyle's mouth, not Kyle. He braces. The arm drives the needles down. They find the ports and find what they were not designed to find — the live nerve clusters under the seal — and pierce them, deep, with the precise, bright pain of an industrial procedure being run on a body that was not the design target. He does not flinch. He has waited longer for worse procedures. Power crosses the interface. The arm's actuators draw current at full draw and fail the first calibration pass — the firmware does not know what kind of body it is bolted to, the legacy interpolation tables are eighteen years out of date — but the E.L.F. is already running the translation, mapping intent through the legacy actuator stack, finding a calibration zero Kyle's nervous system can drive. He gets shoulder, then elbow, then wrist, then individual fingers. Each new joint is a piece of stuffing put back into the Scarecrow. And each new joint costs him pain-relief reserve. The NeoCortex routes pain off the conscious channel for the first ten minutes — buffered against a stockpile of synthetic endorphin analogue the package keeps for crisis moments — and then the stockpile starts draining at a measurable rate, the pain breaking through in pulses Kyle catalogs with the same affectless precision he used on Hua's hands an hour ago. By minute twenty the buffer is at thirty percent. By minute thirty-five the buffer is empty. The needles in his nerve clusters are no longer a precise bright pain — they are a continuous bright pain, and the integration is not finished. He keeps working. The procedure that was bad has become an ad-hoc surgery in a dark, filthy, unsanitary hole — the trench mud six inches from his thigh, organic runoff dripping from the conduit overhead, the cauterizer band's seal compromised at the port row and weeping serous fluid into the seated needles. The NeoCortex flips its priorities the way a triage protocol does: pain stops being a thing the package will pay to dampen, antibiotics start being a thing the package will pay to push. The internal pump goes to overdrive. The package will not let the wound get septic on a night where septic is the difference between making the AutoDoc window and not. He bleeds through the cauterizer seam, sweats, breathes, and continues. Once the arm has hand, the hand finishes the assembly: it loops three turns of salvaged power cable around the arm's rotator stem and Kyle's right forearm, knotted by the new arm's own clumsy fingers. The cauterizer band closes back over the port row, the needles still seated through it. The deal is now physical, electrical, neural, and verbal — *we cooperate* the E.L.F. has said, in his mouth, with his vocal cords — and Kyle understands that he has agreed to a degree of intimacy with this thing that the contracts on the surface do not have a category for. The E.L.F. yields, slowly, as he reclaims motor control: shoulder first, then voice, then mouth, then the cargo arm itself comes under his nervous-system command with the E.L.F. retreating to firmware-side interpolation only. By the time he stands the only thing the E.L.F. is still doing is making his intent legible to the actuators. The arm hangs from his right wrist nearly to the floor. The fingertips drag. He says, aloud, *Are you helping me.* The status strip pulses twice — the same glyph. The mouth is his again. He has been sewn back together by something silent and patient that has been waiting eighteen years for a viable body to fall into the trench.

beats.title: Whatever the Depot Puts in Front of Him
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. The mutant — Depot-stock, two-meter quadruped, jaw plates fused into a single biting beak, three-day-decayed flesh under a chitin sheath — reaches the dry shelf. Kyle has no sword. Silence is upstairs on Hua's table. He has the cargo arm, three meters of corroded conduit pipe leaning against the wall, and a hand-sized shard of cargo crate glass at his foot. He picks the pipe up with the arm — clumsy, the lag visible, the E.L.F. correcting in the firmware — and he steps inside the mutant's lunge. The first swing is bad — too high, too late, the E.L.F. routing around his intent — and the pipe glances off the chitin sheath. The mutant takes him to the wall. Kyle gets the shard of glass into his cauterized left stump end-on, a brutal improvisation that drives the cauterizer band's residual heat into the glass for grip, and brings the shard up under the mutant's beak through the soft seam at the base of the throat. Hot blood, three liters of it, on the shelf. The mutant goes down. Kyle stands over it with the cargo arm holding a length of pipe at low ready, his right stump still bound to a borrowed limb, his left stump bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass is now embedded. He says, aloud, *I am going up.* The status strip pulses twice. He is going up.
beats.location: South sluice dry shelf, Cruciform Depot lower levels
beats.emotional_arc: Earned competence with what the world hands you — the reader feels the dignity of a man who has chosen not to be picky about what he fights with. The improvisation is bushido without a class subsidizing it.
beats.stakes: First proof the borrowed arm is a weapon. First proof Kyle can fight without Silence. The mutant.

beats.title: The Way Up
beats.goal: Kyle and the E.L.F. find a route through the Depot's sealed lower levels back toward the south arm's syndicate chamber. The E.L.F. is leading — through the cargo arm's firmware, through which doors open on which patterns of pressure-plate contact, *and from inside Kyle's NeoCortex stack* now, since the entity has not been in the cargo arm for an hour. Two more mutants are routed around without engagement; the E.L.F. knows the patrol cycles. Kyle stops once on a maintenance landing and asks, aloud: *Why are you helping me.* The status strip on the cargo arm — the only outbound signal channel the E.L.F. uses with him, kept *as a courtesy*, since the E.L.F. could speak through his mouth at any moment without warning — resolves a single firmware glyph into a recognizable shape: the symbol the Cruciform Depot's original Axiom signage used for *salvage rights*. Kyle understands. The E.L.F. is not helping. The E.L.F. is collecting. The collection began an hour ago when the maintenance lead crossed the auditory contact behind his ear; the E.L.F. has been resident in him since then, and the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist is, as of right now, just a tool the resident is using to do the work the resident wants done. The salvage was Kyle. He nods once, in the dark, and they keep climbing. He does not know yet exactly what salvage of him will look like. He has decided he does not need to know yet. The thing that needs to happen first is upstairs, and after that he will renegotiate from a position of having Silence in his hand again.

acts.name: The Return
acts.purpose: Kyle walks back through the Lotus Syndicate's front door, breaks everyone in the room except Hua, takes Silence back from her across her own table, and instead of killing her converts the punishment into a debt: Φ85,000, more than his life is worth, owed to him. beats.title: Front Door
beats.goal: COMBAT BEAT. Kyle walks into the Lotus Syndicate chamber through the front entrance. He does not knock. He does not take an angle. He comes in with the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist nearly to the floor, the fingertips dragging across the flagstones, a length of conduit pipe loose in the borrowed grip and a shard of glass still wedged into his left cauterizer band. Eight men in the room. Hua at the back beside the crocodile tank, and Silence on the table beside her exactly where she left it. The man closest to the door looks at Kyle's silhouette — the dragging arm, the missing hands, the shape of him — and says one word that Kyle does not catalogue. The fight starts. The cargo arm is too long for close work and too slow for fast work; it is a wrecking implement, not a sword arm. Kyle uses it as a wrecking implement: he puts the conduit pipe through the first man's sternum at a swing radius nothing in the room is built to defend against, drives the second backward into the wall by the throat and pins him there long enough to leave him. The third man fires; the round goes into the cargo arm's shoulder housing and the arm holds, the E.L.F. routing power around the failure. Kyle takes the third man with the embedded glass shard under the jaw — fast, ugly, a method he did not have an hour ago. The fourth tries to grapple Kyle inside the cargo arm's reach and Kyle puts him through the glass tank. The crocodile, suddenly free, suddenly awake, attends to the fifth man without further input. *Chekhov's Crocodile,* Kyle thinks, dry, without affect — the NeoCortex flagging the dramatic geometry the way it flags exits. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six and seven go down clean. Eight runs. Kyle does not pursue. Hua is alone behind the table — Kyle has left her there on purpose. Silence is between them.

beats.emotional_arc: The reader feels the discipline restored under impossible constraint — the code holds even when the body practicing it is borrowed and dragging, even when the sword is not in the hand. The fight is ugly because Kyle is fighting with a body that was never his.

beats.title: Eighty-Five Thousand
beats.goal: Hua does not run. She does not reach for Silence. She watches Kyle cross the room, the cargo arm dragging across the flagstones, a track of mutant blood and his own behind him. He stops on the far side of the table from her. Silence is between them, exactly arranged. He brings the cargo arm up and lays the borrowed fingers across the saya, palm down, the way a man claims a thing in front of a witness. Hua puts her own real hand on the blade above his — for one second, for the principle of it. The geometry the chapter has been waiting for: two unaugmented hands meeting on the saya. Except his are in the chum barrel six feet away. The hand in contact with hers is industrial Axiom-era hardware bound to his wrist by salvaged power cable. Kyle waits. She lifts her hand. He picks Silence up with the cargo arm — clumsy, the lag visible, the E.L.F. holding the grip for him so the saya does not slip — and the second he has it the room rebalances. The hamon is cold blue, the bank empty, but the weight is right. He looks at her. He does not raise the blade. The cargo arm holds Silence at a low, formal carry — visible, present, not threatening, the threat already paid down by every man on the floor between them. He says, level: *What was the debt.* Hua opens her mouth. Closes it. Opens it again — her real hands, which she values, are visibly shaking now in a way they were not when she placed the hands of his in the chum barrel. She stutters: *Eighty — eighty-five thousand.* Kyle nods once, as if a piece of arithmetic has resolved. He says: *That's more than my life is worth. So now you owe me.* A pause. *Do you understand.* She nods. The cargo arm does not move. Then — uncharacteristic, ugly, the kind of sound a man makes when something is being taken out of him that he had not catalogued — Kyle screams: *SAY IT.* The room goes quieter than the fight made it. Hua, who has not flinched at a cleaver in this room tonight, flinches at this. She says it. Almost whimpers it: *I owe you.* Kyle does not move for one full breath. Then — discipline back in his voice now, flat, level, colder than the scream was hot — he names the terms: *I'll come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He does not say *you don't get to deem it.* He does not have to. The only mouth in the room that decides when Hua's debt ends is his. Hua nods again, smaller this time, the principle of the gesture from a minute ago entirely gone from it. Then the cargo arm lowers Silence the rest of the way and turns him toward the chum barrel. The arm reaches in and lifts out his two hands, palms up, exactly as Hua placed them. He has a length of twine he scavenged on the way up; the cargo arm loops the twine through the cauterized wrist channels with patient articulation, ties the ends together, and lowers the necklace over his head. The hands hang at the center of his chest, palms outward, dripping. He turns toward the surface without looking at Hua again. Silence is in the cargo arm's grip. Kyle has not let go of it. Hua is alive at her own table.

The scream is the only place in the chapter where Kyle is visibly unguarded; the reader recognizes it as the cost the punishment actually extracted, and it is paid in front of the only person who could measure it.

beats.title: Rain, Then Anesthesia
beats.goal: Kyle climbs through the Cruciform Depot's freight grate and into the rain at street level. He is shaking now — adrenaline gone, bio-battery at 9%, the cargo arm at brownout, Silence still in its borrowed grip. The hands on the necklace knock against his sternum with each step. He walks four blocks in the rain toward the AutoDoc kiosk at the corner of Ashland and Whiting. Two blocks in, his mouth opens — *not because he opened it* — and a voice that is his voice, with the same off-cadence syntax he heard in the trench, says: *I will visit you again.* Kyle does not stop walking. The pace stays exact. He understands what the sentence is doing — confirming a relationship that has not ended, will not end at the AutoDoc, did not end when he stood up from the trench shelf. He asks, flat, his own voice: *What are you called.* A pause. The mouth answers itself: *Puppeteer.* The mouth is his again. Kyle keeps walking. The arithmetic resolves itself in his head with the same dry precision the NeoCortex reserves for catalog work: the cargo arm hanging from his right wrist is empty hardware. The salvage-rights glyph from the lower levels was not a claim against the arm. The salvage was him. Puppeteer is *in him*. Has been since the auditory contact behind his ear was bridged eighteen hours ago, by the count Kyle is now keeping. Will leave when Puppeteer chooses to leave. Will return, *I will visit you again*, on Puppeteer's schedule. He has no leverage and no time to renegotiate. The AutoDoc is still where he is going. He keeps walking. He reaches the kiosk and keys in with his chin. The kiosk reads the necklace. The AutoDoc opens. Inside, the surgical arms unfold and lift him onto the table in the gentle, indifferent way of medical machinery. They take the necklace, they take the cable-bound cargo arm — empty now, shell only — they slide Silence out of the borrowed grip and lay it on the side tray with the careful, automated reverence machines have for swords. They begin the reattachment, the antibiotic pump still running on overdrive, the analgesic finally arriving from the AutoDoc's own dispensary in a dose large enough to mute the night. As the anesthesia goes in, Kyle's NeoCortex feed — *not the cargo arm's status strip, not anymore* — produces a glyph in the same not-factory pattern Puppeteer has been signing in. Three syllables in old Axiom signage. Kyle reads it as he goes under: *we are not done.* The chapter ends on the AutoDoc's status light going green, Silence on the side tray, the rain coming down outside the kiosk, and the sentence still sitting somewhere Kyle cannot easily delete.

The cargo arm's status-strip glyph now resident in his sensorium as a recognizable signature he cannot un-know. The shard of cargo glass he will carry in the cauterizer band until the AutoDoc removes it. character_arcs.want: Out of the trench. Into a body capable of operating on the surface. The cargo arm was never the prize — it was the cell. Kyle is the prize.
character_arcs.need: A host whose cybernetics tolerate full-body puppeting, ideally one who agrees to the arrangement so the host's skills remain intact rather than degraded under hostile possession. Puppeteer's native capability is to seize any cybernetic system effortlessly — but a willing host is operationally superior to a puppeted shell, because the shell loses the trained motor calibration the host's muscles carry. Cooperation is therefore the strategy, not the constraint.
character_arcs.start_state: Trapped in a sealed Axiom-era cargo-handler automaton at the bottom of a Cruciform Depot sluice trench for eighteen years. Cranial broadcast antenna structurally fused. The only outbound signal it can generate is a 19Hz hum at the frequency of the remaining antenna stub. Cannot escape because there is nothing within possession range to jump to — the trench is a cage of distance, not architecture. The mutants of the lower levels are not cybernetic and therefore not viable hosts.
character_arcs.end_state: Resident in Kyle Ellen Corbin-Vasik's NeoCortex stack since the maintenance lead bridged his auditory induction contact in beat 4. Has revealed its name in beat 9 (*Puppeteer*) and announced ongoing access (*I will visit you again*). The cargo arm taken by the AutoDoc is empty hardware. Puppeteer is on the surface, in a viable host, with a cooperative arrangement.
character_arcs.turning_point: Beat 4 — extruding the maintenance lead from the cargo arm's cable bundle to Kyle's exposed left ear, crossing into Kyle's NeoCortex via the auditory induction contact. The instant of escape from eighteen years of imprisonment. Everything subsequent is Puppeteer establishing a working relationship with the host it just possessed.
character_arcs.cost: Disclosure. By the end of beat 9 Kyle has been told the name (*Puppeteer*), the schedule (*I will visit you again*), and — by inference — the capability (effortless possession of any cybernetic entity). What was hidden as long as Puppeteer was sealed in the automaton is now known to a man with a sword and a discipline. Puppeteer has traded eighteen years of secrecy for surface mobility. The ledger is even by Puppeteer's own arithmetic, but the secrecy is gone.

Beats.Title: Accusation
Beats.Text:
The crocodile does not move. Kyle has been watching it for four minutes — the NeoCortex timestamps involuntarily, a facility habit he never unlearned — and the animal has not moved once, its jaw resting on the heat rock with the particular stillness of something that has learned patience as a survival strategy. He understands that. The tank glass is clean. Someone wipes it daily. That detail costs more than the crocodile.

*The smell is chum and bleach and something underneath both that he is choosing not to identify.*

Hua's hands are the first thing he catalogued when they brought him in, before the chair, before the table, before the long lacquered surface where Silence lay with its friction sheath unbuckled and set beside it like a deed already filed. Real skin. Real nails, cut short and unpainted. The NeoCortex flagged them the same way it flags fire exits and secondary egress points — as a structural anomaly in an environment where chrome is the baseline. In the Gray Zone, unaugmented hands mean poverty or principle. In this room, at this table, they mean neither. They mean she does not need to be faster than anyone in the room, because everyone in the room is afraid of her, which is the only speed that matters.

*His hands are the same category of object for a completely different reason, and she does not know that yet, and he is not going to tell her.*

She stops pacing in front of the tank. The two men at his shoulders have not moved in ninety seconds. The toolkit on the floor between them is a black nylon roll, the kind that fastens with two snaps and opens flat, and Kyle has not looked directly at it because looking at it is information he is not yet prepared to have. Silence is on the table. The angle Hua arranged it — parallel to the table edge, saya toward her, handle toward the room's center — is the arrangement of something already appraised.
